newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-MUSTER, CHANG REACH QUARTERS OF CHAMPIONS CUP.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MUSTER, CHANG REACH QUARTERS OF CHAMPIONS CUP.

text.p: Second seed Thomas Muster of Austria and third seed Michael Chang of the United States moved into the quarter-finals of the Champions Cup with straight-set victories Thursday.
In the only third-round battle between seeded players, the defending champion and third-ranked Chang posted a 6-2 7-5 victory over 13th seed Marc Rosset of Switzerland.
The second-ranked Muster disposed of 59th-ranked Czech Slava Dosedel 6-4 6-4.
In the quarters, Muster meets 32nd-ranked Mark "Scud" Philippoussis of Australia, who delivered the fastest serve ever recorded -- 142 mph (228.5 kph) -- last week at the Scottsdale tournament.
Philippoussis sent eighth seed Carlos Moya of Spain, a finalist at this year's Australian Open, packing with a 6-4 6-3 win.

The other quarter-finals pit Chang against 30th-ranked Cedric Pioline of France, 14th seed Alberto Berasategui of Spain against 35th-ranked Jonas Bjorkman of Sweden, and 43rd-ranked Bohdan Ulihrach of the Czech Republic, who upset top seed Pete Sampras in the second round, against 31st-ranked Byron Black of Zimbabwe.
Chang wasn't shy about his chances of successfully defending his Champions Cup title.
"I plan on it," Chang said. "I just take things match by match, but definitely go out there with the faith that I'm going to be there on Sunday, winning the title.."

Chang, who has won this title twice, is only 5 feet 9 inches (1.75 meters) tall and is dwarfed by the 6-foot-7 (2.01 meters) Rosset. But the difference in their size in no way intimidated Chang. Nor did Rosset's 4-2 career advantage over him.
Chang is riding high this year with a 14-2 won-lost record which includes a tournament victory at Memphis two weeks ago.
Rosset's serve can be daunting at its peak but against Chang it was hardly a formidable weapon. Rosset made only 48 percent of his first serves in the one hour, 49 minute contest.
Chang ended the day serving more aces than Rosset -- seven to three. Rosset also double faulted nine times.
"I think it's (my serve) improved tremendously," Chang said. "I feel like it no longer is just a way of starting a point for me."
After exchanging service breaks in the first two games of the match, Chang broke Rosset's serve twice more in the first set.

In the second set, Rosset was serving to go ahead 5-3, but never had a game point in that eighth game. Chang captured the final service break in the last game, winning on a third match point when Rosset blasted a backhand long.

Muster is a noted clay court specialist but all four tournament he has played this year have been on hardcourts. He reached the quarter-finals at Doha, the semifinals at the Australian Open and won in Dubai.
"It's (hardcourts) not my best surface," Muster said. "I've won more tournaments on clay, that's a reality. There's no reason for me to mentally go on hardcourt and say, I can't play on it."
